course: Small Machines & Pharmaceuticals: The Complete Import Business

lessons.title: Understanding the Harmonized System
lessons.body: The Harmonized System (HS) is a standardized numerical method of classifying traded products. It is used by customs authorities worldwide to identify products for duty and tax purposes. Every product you import has an HS code, which is a string of numbers. The first six digits are the same in all countries that use the HS (over 200 countries). The next digits can vary by country. For example, a diesel engine might be 8408.90 in one country and 8408.90.00 in another. The HS is maintained by the World Customs Organization (WCO). It is updated every five years; the current version is HS 2022. As an importer, you must know the HS code of your product because it determines the duty rate, any restrictions, and the documents required. In Africa, most countries use the HS but have their own national tariff schedules. For instance, Nigeria uses the ECOWAS Common External Tariff (CET), which is based on HS 2017. Kenya uses the EAC CET. Ghana uses the ECOWAS CET. These tariffs list the duty rate for each HS code. You can find your country's tariff online or at the customs office. The HS is organized into 21 sections, 97 chapters (chapter 77 is reserved for future use). Chapters are grouped by product type: live animals (01-05), vegetable products (06-14), machinery (84-85), vehicles (86-89), etc. Pharmaceuticals are in Chapter 30. When you import, you must declare the HS code on your customs declaration. If you misclassify, you may pay the wrong duty or face penalties. So, it's crucial to get it right. Start by understanding the structure: the first two digits are the chapter, the next two are the heading, and the next two are the subheading. For example, 3004.90 is a subheading for medicaments. In the next lessons, we'll show you how to find the exact code for your product and calculate your taxes.

lessons.title: Finding the Correct HS Code for Your Product
lessons.body: Finding the correct HS code can be tricky, but with the right tools and method, you can do it. First, gather details about your product: what it is, what it's made of, its function, and its packaging. For example, a portable generator: is it diesel or petrol? What is its power output? These details matter. Next, use online resources. The WCO has a free HS database (https://www.wcotradetools.org/en/harmonized-system). Your country's customs website often has a tariff finder. For Nigeria, use the Nigeria Customs Service Trade Portal. For Kenya, use the Kenya Trade Network Agency (KenTrade) portal. For Ghana, use the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) online tariff. These tools let you search by keyword or browse chapters. Start with the chapter that seems most relevant. For machinery, look at Chapters 84 and 85. Chapter 84 covers mechanical appliances, boilers, and engines. Chapter 85 covers electrical machinery. For pharmaceuticals, Chapter 30. Once you find a potential code, read the description carefully. The HS uses a hierarchy: Section, Chapter, Heading, Subheading. You must match your product to the most specific description. For example, if you import a laptop, it's not just 'machinery' (Chapter 84) but specifically 8471.30 for portable digital computers. If you import a solar panel, it's 8541.40. If you import paracetamol tablets, it's 3004.90 (medicaments). If you're unsure, you can request a binding ruling from customs. In many African countries, you can submit a sample or detailed description and get an official classification. This is free and legally binding. Also, ask other importers or customs brokers. They have practical experience. But beware: using the wrong code can lead to fines or delays. For example, in Kenya, misclassification can result in a penalty of 25% of the duty. So, double-check. Finally, document your classification. Keep a record of why you chose that code. This helps if customs questions you later. Remember, the HS code is the foundation of your import taxes, so invest time in getting it right.

lessons.title: Import Duty Rates for Machinery in Your Country
lessons.body: Import duty rates for machinery vary by country and by type of machine. In most African countries, machinery for industrial use often attracts lower duty rates than consumer goods. For example, in Nigeria, under the ECOWAS CET, many machinery items in Chapters 84 and 85 have a duty rate of 5% or 10%. But some items, like used machinery, may attract higher rates or even be prohibited. In Kenya, under the EAC CET, duty rates for machinery are typically 0% or 10% for capital goods, but 25% for some finished goods. In Ghana, the ECOWAS CET applies, so similar rates. However, there are exceptions. For instance, generators (HS 8502) might have a duty rate of 10% in Nigeria, but in Kenya, solar generators (HS 8501.31) might be 0% to promote renewable energy. You must check your country's tariff schedule for the exact HS code. Also, consider that some machinery may be exempt from duty if it's for agricultural or medical use. For example, in many countries, tractors (HS 8701) are duty-free. Similarly, machinery for manufacturing pharmaceuticals may be duty-free under investment incentives. To find the rate, go to your customs website or use the tariff finder. For Nigeria, the Nigeria Customs Service has a tariff search. For Kenya, the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) has an online tariff. For Ghana, the GRA has a tariff portal. You can also visit a customs office and ask for the current tariff book. Once you know the duty rate, you can calculate the duty amount: Duty = (CIF Value) x Duty Rate. CIF is Cost, Insurance, Freight. So, if you import a machine for $10,000 CIF and duty is 10%, you pay $1,000. But watch out for additional taxes like VAT and levies. In the next lessons, we'll cover those. Also, note that duty rates can change. Check before you import. And consider using a customs broker to ensure you get the right rate. They know the latest changes and can help you avoid overpaying.

lessons.title: Import Duty Rates for Pharmaceuticals
lessons.body: Pharmaceuticals are essential goods, and many African countries offer reduced or zero import duty on them. In Nigeria, under the ECOWAS CET, most medicaments (HS 3004) have a duty rate of 0% or 5%. For example, paracetamol tablets (HS 3004.90) are often 0% duty. In Kenya, under the EAC CET, pharmaceuticals are generally duty-free (0%) to make healthcare affordable. In Ghana, the ECOWAS CET also sets duty at 0% for most pharmaceuticals. However, there are exceptions. Some countries impose duty on certain categories, like veterinary pharmaceuticals or cosmetics that contain medicinal ingredients. Also, raw materials for making pharmaceuticals (active ingredients) may have different rates. For instance, in Nigeria, some active ingredients (HS 2941) may attract 5% duty. You must check the specific HS code. Additionally, some countries require an import permit from the health ministry or drug regulatory agency. For example, in Nigeria, you need a permit from NAFDAC. In Kenya, from the Pharmacy and Poisons Board. In Ghana, from the Food and Drugs Authority. These permits are separate from customs. To find the duty rate, use your country's tariff finder. For Nigeria, search the NCS tariff for Chapter 30. For Kenya, use the KRA tariff. For Ghana, use the GRA tariff. You can also consult a customs broker who specializes in pharmaceuticals. They know the nuances. Also, note that even if duty is 0%, you may still pay VAT and other levies. For example, in Kenya, VAT on pharmaceuticals is 0% (exempt), but in Nigeria, VAT is 7.5% on most goods, though some pharmaceuticals may be exempt. So, always check the full tax picture. Finally, consider that donated pharmaceuticals may have different procedures. If you're importing for commercial purposes, ensure you have all documents: invoice, packing list, bill of lading, permit, and certificate of analysis. This will speed up clearance. In summary, pharmaceuticals often enjoy low or zero duty, but you must verify and comply with health regulations.

lessons.title: VAT and Other Levies
lessons.body: When importing, you pay more than just import duty. Value Added Tax (VAT) is a consumption tax applied to most goods and services. In many African countries, VAT is charged on the CIF value plus import duty. So, if your goods cost $10,000 CIF and duty is $1,000, VAT is calculated on $11,000. VAT rates vary: Nigeria 7.5%, Kenya 16%, Ghana 15% (plus NHIL and GETFund levies). However, some goods are exempt or zero-rated. In Kenya, pharmaceuticals and agricultural inputs are VAT-exempt. In Nigeria, basic food items and medical products may be exempt. In Ghana, some machinery for manufacturing may be exempt. You must check your country's VAT Act. Besides VAT, there are other levies. In Nigeria, there's a 0.5% ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme (ETLS) levy, and a 0.5% Comprehensive Import Supervision Scheme (CISS) levy. In Kenya, there's a 2% Import Declaration Fee (IDF) and a 1.5% Railway Development Levy (RDL). In Ghana, there are NHIL (2.5%), GETFund (2.5%), and COVID-19 levy (1%). These add up. So, your total tax can be significant. To calculate, use this formula: Total Taxes = Import Duty + VAT + Other Levies. For example, in Kenya, if CIF is $10,000, duty 10% = $1,000, IDF 2% = $200, RDL 1.5% = $150, VAT 16% on ($10,000+$1,000) = $1,760. Total taxes = $3,110. That's a lot! So, you must factor these into your landed cost. Also, some countries offer exemptions or reduced rates for certain imports, like machinery for export processing zones. Check if you qualify. To pay, you usually pay through the customs system or a bank. Keep all receipts. If you overpay, you can claim a refund, but it's a hassle. So, get it right the first time. Use a customs broker to help you compute and pay the correct taxes. They can also advise on exemptions. Remember, VAT is often recoverable if you're VAT-registered and sell the goods, but for many small importers, it's a cost. So, plan your pricing accordingly.

lessons.title: Calculating Your True Landed Cost
lessons.body: Landed cost is the total cost of a product once it has arrived at your door, including the product cost, shipping, insurance, customs duties, taxes, and other fees. Many importers make the mistake of only looking at the product price and shipping, then get shocked by customs charges. To calculate your true landed cost, follow these steps. First, determine the FOB (Free On Board) price from your supplier. This is the cost of the goods plus loading onto the ship at the port of origin. Second, add international freight and insurance. Freight can be air or sea. For sea, a 20-foot container from China to Nigeria might cost $3,000-$5,000. Insurance is usually 0.5% of FOB. This gives you CIF (Cost, Insurance, Freight). Third, calculate import duty. Use the HS code and your country's duty rate. Duty = CIF x Duty Rate. Fourth, calculate VAT. VAT = (CIF + Duty) x VAT Rate. Fifth, add other levies like IDF, RDL, ETLS, etc. Sixth, add port charges, clearing agent fees, transportation to your warehouse, and any demurrage if delays. Also, consider bank charges for foreign exchange and letters of credit. Once you sum all these, you get the landed cost. For example, importing a machine: FOB $10,000, freight $1,000, insurance $50, CIF $11,050. Duty at 10% = $1,105. VAT at 16% on $12,155 = $1,945. IDF 2% = $221, RDL 1.5% = $166. Clearing agent $500, transport $200. Total landed cost = $11,050 + $1,105 + $1,945 + $221 + $166 + $500 + $200 = $15,187. That's 52% more than FOB! So, you must price your product with this in mind. To make a profit, your selling price must exceed landed cost plus your operating expenses and desired margin. Use a spreadsheet to compute this for each product. Also, consider exchange rate fluctuations; they can significantly affect your cost. Always get a recent quote from your freight forwarder and customs broker. Tools like the online landed cost calculators from freight forwarders can help. But verify the rates with your local customs. In Africa, it's wise to add a 10-15% buffer for unexpected charges. By knowing your true landed cost, you can negotiate better with suppliers, choose the most cost-effective shipping method, and set profitable prices.

quiz.q: What is the Harmonized System (HS)?
options: A) A global system for classifying traded products
B) A type of import duty
quiz.explanation: The HS is a standardized numerical method of classifying traded products, used by customs worldwide.

quiz.q: How many digits of the HS code are the same in all countries?
quiz.explanation: The first six digits of the HS code are harmonized internationally; additional digits can vary by country.

quiz.q: Which chapter of the HS covers pharmaceuticals?
quiz.explanation: Pharmaceutical products are classified under HS Chapter 30.

quiz.q: What is the first step in finding the correct HS code for your product?
quiz.explanation: You need to know what your product is made of, its function, and other details to classify it correctly.

quiz.q: Which of these is a free online tool for finding HS codes?
quiz.explanation: The World Customs Organization provides a free HS database through WCO Trade Tools.

quiz.q: What is a binding ruling?
options: A) A legal decision on classification by customs
B) A contract with a supplier
quiz.explanation: A binding ruling is an official decision by customs on the classification of your goods, which is legally binding.

quiz.q: In Nigeria, what is the duty rate for most machinery under the ECOWAS CET?
quiz.explanation: Many machinery items in Chapters 84 and 85 have a duty rate of 5% or 10% in Nigeria.

quiz.q: Which of these is a capital good that often enjoys 0% duty in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: Kenya often grants 0% duty on solar generators to promote renewable energy.

quiz.q: What is CIF?
quiz.explanation: CIF stands for Cost, Insurance, and Freight, and is the value used to calculate import duty.

quiz.q: How is import duty calculated?
quiz.explanation: Import duty is calculated as a percentage of the CIF value.

quiz.q: In Nigeria, what is the duty rate for paracetamol tablets (HS 3004.90)?
quiz.explanation: Most medicaments in Nigeria have a duty rate of 0% or 5% under the ECOWAS CET.

quiz.q: Which agency must you get a permit from to import pharmaceuticals in Nigeria?
quiz.explanation: NAFDAC regulates pharmaceuticals in Nigeria and requires an import permit.

quiz.q: In Kenya, what is the VAT rate on most goods?
quiz.explanation: Kenya's standard VAT rate is 16%.

quiz.q: What is the VAT rate in Nigeria?
quiz.explanation: Nigeria's VAT rate is 7.5%.

quiz.q: Which of these is a levy charged on imports in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: Kenya charges an Import Declaration Fee (IDF) of 2% on imports.

quiz.q: How is VAT calculated on imports?
quiz.explanation: VAT is applied to the sum of the CIF value and import duty.

quiz.q: What does landed cost include?
options: C) All costs to get the product to your door
quiz.explanation: Landed cost includes product cost, shipping, insurance, duties, taxes, and other fees.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT typically part of landed cost?
quiz.explanation: The supplier's profit margin is included in the FOB price, not a separate landed cost item.

quiz.q: Why is it important to calculate true landed cost?
options: A) To set profitable selling prices
C) To get a binding ruling
quiz.explanation: Knowing your true landed cost helps you price your products to ensure profitability.

quiz.q: What is the HS code for portable digital computers (laptops)?
quiz.explanation: Laptops are classified under HS 8471.30.

quiz.q: In Ghana, which of these levies is charged on imports?
quiz.explanation: Ghana charges the National Health Insurance Levy (NHIL) on imports.

quiz.q: What is the penalty for misclassification in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: In Kenya, misclassification can result in a penalty of 25% of the duty.

quiz.q: Which of these is a source for finding duty rates in Nigeria?
options: A) Nigeria Customs Service Trade Portal
quiz.explanation: The Nigeria Customs Service Trade Portal provides tariff information for Nigeria.

quiz.q: What is the duty rate for tractors in many African countries?
quiz.explanation: Many countries exempt tractors from import duty to support agriculture.

quiz.q: Which of these is a document required for importing pharmaceuticals?
quiz.explanation: All these documents are typically required for importing pharmaceuticals.

quiz.q: What is the VAT treatment of pharmaceuticals in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: Pharmaceuticals are VAT-exempt in Kenya.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common mistake importers make?
quiz.explanation: Many importers only consider product and shipping costs, ignoring duties and taxes.

quiz.q: What is the first step in calculating landed cost?
quiz.explanation: Start with the FOB price from your supplier, then add freight, insurance, and other costs.

quiz.q: In Ghana, what is the VAT rate?
quiz.explanation: Ghana's standard VAT rate is 15%.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a record of your HS classification?
options: A) To show customs if questioned
quiz.explanation: Documenting your classification helps justify your choice if customs audits your imports.
